cultural_notes: Woccon is a Native American tribe located in the Carolinas
Documented by multiple European sources from 1521-1795
Referred to by numerous variant names including Guacaya, Wococon, Wokakon, Woccoa
Known as 'Northward's Indians' and 'Parched Corn Indians'
Multiple historical maps and colonial documents reference this tribe
Likely a Siouan-speaking group based on linguistic classification
Woccon belonged to the Siouan linguistic stock, closest to Catawba
Primarily lived between Neuse River and its affluents, near present-day Goldsboro, Wayne County, North Carolina
Villages included Tooptatmeer and Yupwauremau, both supposed to be in Greene County
First documented by Lawson around 1701, who recorded 150 words of their language
Estimated population of 600 in 1600, with 120 warriors in 1701
Participated in Tuscarora Wars (1711-1715)
Likely extinguished as a tribe during Tuscarora Wars, with survivors potentially fleeing north with Tuscarora, joining Catawba, or combining with other Siouan groups
Only southern eastern Siouan tribe besides Catawba with a preserved vocabulary
Woccon is likely related to Waccamaw people
Historically located in coastal regions of North and South Carolina
Experienced significant disruption from Spanish entrada in 16th-17th centuries
Shared ties with Cheraw/Saraw, Waccamaw of NC, Lumbee, Cape Fear, and Catawba tribes
Documented by early European explorers like Francisco Gordillo (1521) and William Hilton (1662-1663)
By 1670, English sources identified them living along Waccamaw and PeeDee Rivers
Woccon are a Siouan language group identified by John Lawson in 1701
Lawson recorded 120 fighting men and 500 total inhabitants in two towns: Yupwareremau and Tooptatmeer
In 1699, Richard Traunter described them as 'Caniballs, and Maneaters'
Participated in Tuscarora War (1711-1713) alongside Barnwell's forces
Woccon name disappears around the same time Waccamaw name appears
Two Woccon were arrested in Virginia for leaving North Carolina without permission
Documented by early colonial sources like John Lawson's 'New Voyage to Carolina'
Woccon were closely associated with Cape Fear tribes
In 1712, Waccamaw and Cape Fear tribes were allies with James Moore JR. against the Tuscarora
In 1715, Waccamaw had 610 people living near Pee Dee River
During the 1715 Yamassee War, Waccamaw joined Yamassee and Cheraw in attacking South Carolina
In 1715, they were defeated by Maurice Moore and many were taken captive/enslaved
Source of historical information: John Swanton, Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin (1952)
Waccamaw people lived between Black and Sampit Rivers at Winyah Bay
Had approximately 100 fighting men in 1718
Experienced conflict with colonial authorities in 1718 Waccamaw War
Located in South Carolina region near Charleston
Traded with colonial factors like William Waties and Meredith Hughes
Interacted with other Indigenous groups like Charraws and Catawba
Waccamaw were a Native American group operating independently with several hundred people
Cooperated with Catawba nation
Faced raids and enslavement by Seneca and Cherokee groups
Sought refuge with Winyaw and Pedee in 1723
Historically located on Lumber River in North Carolina
Experienced displacement by local planters like King Roger Moore in 1725
Potentially incorporated with Catawba nation, though absorption by English settlements is also possible
Documented by anthropologists and historians like Mooney (1894), Hodge (1910), and Swanton (1952)
Waccamaw are a Siouan-speaking tribe located in South Carolina and North Carolina
Historically documented from 1728-1850 in historical records
Inhabited areas around Lake Waccamaw and Dog Bluff region
Experienced significant displacement and cultural disruption in 18th-19th centuries
By 1755 referred to as 'Settlement Indians'
Many fled to North Carolina swamps in 1778
Dimery family was a prominent community lineage
Maintained community through church establishments like Dimery Church and Holly Hill Free Will Baptist Church
Woccon was a language within the Siouan linguistic family
Woccon was most closely related to Catawba
Eastern Siouan branch includes Catawba and Woccon languages
Modern tribal recognition occurred in 2005
Tribal organizational meeting was on October 17th, 1992
Tribal grounds land was purchased in 2004
HR1942 was signed in 2021
Woccon is an Eastern Siouan language
Woccon closely resembled Catawba and was considered one of two Catahban languages
Waccon was a subdivision of the Waccamaw
Waccamaw territory extended from Winyah Bay up Waccamaw River to the Cape Fear, and somewhat to the Neuse River
Language documentation sources include Adelung & Vater (1806), Carter (1980), Lawson (1709), and recent linguistic conference proceedings

Woccon is a Siouan language from the coastal Carolina region
Documented in scholarly linguistic sources like Rudes (2000) in Southern Journal of Linguistics
